::: {.callout-important}
All code on this page is example code — adapt every step to your own study variables before running. Field IDs, category codes, and column names used here are illustrations.
:::

This page walks through [`scripts/manage_dataset.R`](https://github.com/saras-clin/UKB_help/blob/main/scripts/manage_dataset.R).

---

## Step 1: Inspect

Run `dplyr::glimpse(dataset)` before making any changes. It shows all column names, their R types, and a sample of values. UKB columns follow a `p<FieldID>` naming convention — look up any Field ID on the [UK Biobank Data Showcase](https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/).

---

## Step 2: Rename variables

Renaming `p31`, `p34_i0` etc. to descriptive names makes the rest of the script readable. Only columns present in your dataset need an entry — the `renames_present` filter prevents errors for fields you did not extract.

```r
rename_variables <- function(data) {
  renames <- c(
    sex                     = "p31",
    year_birth              = "p34",
    month_birth             = "p52",
    date_baseline           = "p53_i0",
    date_lost_to_followup   = "p191",
    current_tobacco_smoking = "p1239_i0",
    ethnicity               = "p21000_i0",
    physical_activity       = "p22032_i0"
  )
  renames_present <- renames[renames %in% names(data)]
  dplyr::rename(data, dplyr::all_of(renames_present))
}
```

---

## Step 3: Convert variable types

Check types with `glimpse()` in Step 1 first, then keep only the conversions your data actually needs. `eid` should always be integer for safe joins.

::: {.callout-warning}
A mismatch between integer and character `eid` silently produces zero rows after a join — no error, no warning.
:::

---

## Step 4: Recode categorical variables to factors

UKB stores categoricals as integers (e.g. 0 = Female, 1 = Male). Converting to factor with labels makes tables and plots self-documenting.

UKB uses negative codes for special responses: **-1** = Do not know, **-3** = Prefer not to answer. These are distinct from `NA` (not asked / not linked) and should get explicit labels.

`case_when()` assigns the label from the first matching condition. The `TRUE ~ "Unknown"` line at the end catches anything not explicitly handled — a large "Unknown" count means codes in your data are missing from the blocks. Check with:

```r
table(dataset$sex, useNA = "ifany")      # raw codes
table(dataset$sex_cat, useNA = "ifany")  # after recoding
```

The ethnicity field uses a hierarchical coding scheme — both parent codes (e.g. `1` = White) and sub-codes (e.g. `1001` = British) appear depending on what the participant selected. Group them together.

---

## Step 5: Create derived variables

UKB provides year and month of birth but not day. Using the 15th of the month is standard practice — be aware this introduces up to 15 days of error in age calculations.

```r
date_birth   = as.Date(paste(year_birth, sprintf("%02d", month_birth), "15", sep = "-"))
age_baseline = as.numeric(difftime(date_baseline, date_birth, units = "days")) / 365.25
```

UKB recruited participants aged 40–69 at baseline (2006–2010). Calculated ages outside this range indicate a parsing error.

---

## Step 6: Data quality checks

**Duplicate eids** — each participant should appear once. Duplicates usually come from a one-to-many join in `setup.R`.

**Missingness** — high missingness in core variables (sex, age, date_baseline) is unusual. High missingness in optional fields (physical activity, dietary measures) is expected — these questions were not asked at every instance.

**Implausible values** — check `range(dataset$age_baseline, na.rm = TRUE)` against the expected 40–69 range, and `max(dataset$date_baseline, na.rm = TRUE)` to confirm no future dates.
